title: The Science of Break-Ups
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the science of breakups: timing spikes (early December, early March, spring break), who initiates and how (in person vs. text/email, generational differences), gender differences in explaining breakups, depression after being dumped, attachment styles, a 2011 Einstein College of Medicine brain imaging study showing photos of an ex activate pain and addiction-related brain regions, the dopamine-and-sadness cycle, getting back together, marriage and time as factors in relationship longevity, stress-related growth and identity after breakups, Northwestern forecasting study on breakup severity, psychologist Guy Winch's recovery tips, a Journal of Experimental Psychology study comparing recovery strategies, and why sad songs help. The episode ends with an ad-style segment featuring Matt and Joel of the How to Money podcast discussing personal finance topics, beer, and debt.

entities.name: How to Fix a Broken Heart

segments.title: Opening and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh introduces the breakup episode, mentions a How to Money segment coming at the end, and explains that listeners who are heartbroken prompted the topic.

segments.title: Marriage timing and breakup spikes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how later marriage may mean more breakups, a study finding most people will experience a breakup, and that Facebook data suggests breakups spike in early December and early March around holidays and spring break.

segments.title: Who breaks up and how
segments.summary: Being dumped is harder than dumping because the initiator has already gone through a long decision process. Holiday pressure and gift-giving are cited as reasons to break up before the holidays. The hosts discuss breakup methods by generation, with in-person breakups declining and phone and text increasing, and email rated worst.

segments.title: Gender differences and depression after breakups
segments.summary: Women tend to present lists of grievances while men are more nebulous, a generalization the hosts caution against. Breakups can cause depression, anxiety, and in rare cases suicidal or homicidal thoughts. An eight-week follow-up found signs of clinical depression still present and twelve percent moderately or severely depressed.

segments.title: Attachment styles and divorce initiation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss attachment styles, anxious and avoidant, as a spectrum rather than gender-based traits. A self-reported Venn-diagram style scale is described. They note that about two-thirds of women initiate divorces, and question how that affects recovery.

segments.title: Brain imaging study of ex photos
segments.summary: A 2011 Einstein College of Medicine study with Rutgers anthropologists found that looking at a photo of an ex activated pain-processing brain regions and regions tied to addiction cravings. The cycle involves a dopamine reward, then sadness, then urges to contact the ex, then frustration from the prefrontal cortex. Follow-up work by Helen Fisher found these responses decline over time.

segments.title: Social media and Guy Winch's advice
segments.summary: Psychologist Guy Winch advises staying off social media and avoiding checking on an ex, since this keeps the ex in mind and prolongs recovery. The hosts discuss how the breakup can make people feel that they want to be in contact.
topics: How to Fix a Broken Heart

segments.title: Getting back together and rehashing the relationship
segments.summary: People tend to rehash relationships by remembering the good parts and forgetting the bad. Getting back together without changing underlying personalities and conflict scripts often repeats the same problems. Many younger people reportedly get back together multiple times.

segments.title: Marriage, time, and relationship longevity
segments.summary: A study found the greatest risk of breakup is in the first year or two for all couples, with marriage and time as key factors for staying together. The hosts doubt the very low divorce figure given the high overall divorce rate. Relationships are discussed in terms of losing some sense of self.

segments.title: Stress-related growth, rejection, and recovery tips
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how growth during a relationship can make breakups harder, and how people who blame a personal flaw should instead pursue stress-related growth. Guy Winch's tips include listing compromises you don't want to repeat, returning to former enjoyable activities, removing reminders, and reconnecting with friends. A Northwestern study found people expected breakups to be worse than they were.

segments.title: Recovery strategies study and sad songs
segments.summary: A Journal of Experimental Psychology study tested reappraisal, love reappraisal, distraction, and a control condition using EEG and photos of exes; all three strategies reduced emotional response relative to control, but distraction did not reduce long-term recovery. Other tips include writing an unsent letter and why sad songs help people process emotion.
